data.scenario_text: The function L(x)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)\right]+12 models the number of hours of daylight in a city in the Northern Hemisphere, where x=1 represents January, x=2 represents February, and so on.
data.part_a: What is the average number of hours of daylight in this city over the year?
data.part_b: What is the range of the number of hours of daylight in this city?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in November. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=2, so the quantity rises 2 above the average value and falls 2 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

The longest day is in June, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in December, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in March, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in June and the shortest in December, as expected in the Northern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=11 (November):

L(11)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(11-3)\right]+12=2\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)+12

=2\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+12=-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{2}+12

So the model gives approximately \boxed{10.3\text{ hr}} of daylight in November.

data.part_b: What is the range of the number of hours of daylight in this city?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in May. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=2, so the quantity rises 2 above the average value and falls 2 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

The longest day is in June, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in December, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in March, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in June and the shortest in December, as expected in the Northern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=5 (May):

L(5)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(5-3)\right]+12=2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+12

=2\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+12=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{2}+12

So the model gives approximately \boxed{13.7\text{ hr}} of daylight in May.

data.part_b: What is the range of the number of hours of daylight in this city?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in May. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=2, so the quantity rises 2 above the average value and falls 2 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

The longest day is in June, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in December, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in March, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in June and the shortest in December, as expected in the Northern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=5 (May):

L(5)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(5-3)\right]+12=2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+12

=2\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+12=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{2}+12

So the model gives approximately \boxed{13.7\text{ hr}} of daylight in May.

data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in October. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=2, so the quantity rises 2 above the average value and falls 2 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

The longest day is in December, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in June, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-9)=0 \implies x-9=0 \implies x=9

The phase shift is \boxed{9} months, and so the pattern is shifted 9 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in September, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in December and the shortest in June, as expected in the Southern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (October):

L(10)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-9)\right]+12=2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+12

=2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=13

So the model gives exactly \boxed{13.0\text{ hr}} of daylight in October.

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ hr}

data.part_b: What is the range of the number of hours of daylight in this city?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in October. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=2, so the quantity rises 2 above the average value and falls 2 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

The longest day is in December, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in June, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-9)=0 \implies x-9=0 \implies x=9

The phase shift is \boxed{9} months, and so the pattern is shifted 9 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in September, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in December and the shortest in June, as expected in the Southern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (October):

L(10)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-9)\right]+12=2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+12

=2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=13

So the model gives exactly \boxed{13.0\text{ hr}} of daylight in October.

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

data.part_b: What is the range of the number of hours of daylight in this city?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in November. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=2, so the quantity rises 2 above the average value and falls 2 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

The longest day is in June, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in December, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in March, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in June and the shortest in December, as expected in the Northern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=11 (November):

L(11)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(11-3)\right]+12=2\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)+12

=2\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+12=-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{2}+12

So the model gives approximately \boxed{10.3\text{ hr}} of daylight in November.

data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in October. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=2, so the quantity rises 2 above the average value and falls 2 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

The longest day is in December, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in June, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-9)=0 \implies x-9=0 \implies x=9

The phase shift is \boxed{9} months, and so the pattern is shifted 9 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in September, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in December and the shortest in June, as expected in the Southern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (October):

L(10)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-9)\right]+12=2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+12

=2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=13

So the model gives exactly \boxed{13.0\text{ hr}} of daylight in October.

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in October. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=2, so the quantity rises 2 above the average value and falls 2 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

The longest day is in December, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in June, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-9)=0 \implies x-9=0 \implies x=9

The phase shift is \boxed{9} months, and so the pattern is shifted 9 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in September, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in December and the shortest in June, as expected in the Southern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (October):

L(10)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-9)\right]+12=2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+12

=2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=13

So the model gives exactly \boxed{13.0\text{ hr}} of daylight in October.

Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=2, so the quantity rises 2 above the average value and falls 2 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

The longest day is in December, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in June, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in July. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ hr}

The longest day is in June, with 16\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in December, with 8\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[8\text{ hr},\ 16\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in March, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in June and the shortest in December, as expected in the Northern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=7 (July):

L(7)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-3)\right]+12=4\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)+12

=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+12=\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{2}+12

So the model gives approximately \boxed{15.5\text{ hr}} of daylight in July.

data.part_b: What is the range of the number of hours of daylight in this city?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in October. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=2, so the quantity rises 2 above the average value and falls 2 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

The longest day is in June, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in December, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in March, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in June and the shortest in December, as expected in the Northern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (October):

L(10)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-3)\right]+12=2\sin\left(\frac{7\pi}{6}\right)+12

=2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=11

So the model gives exactly \boxed{11.0\text{ hr}} of daylight in October.

data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in October. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=2, so the quantity rises 2 above the average value and falls 2 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+2=14\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-2=10\text{ hr}

The longest day is in December, with 14\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in June, with 10\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[10\text{ hr},\ 14\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-9)=0 \implies x-9=0 \implies x=9

The phase shift is \boxed{9} months, and so the pattern is shifted 9 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in September, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in December and the shortest in June, as expected in the Southern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (October):

L(10)=2\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-9)\right]+12=2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+12

=2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=13

So the model gives exactly \boxed{13.0\text{ hr}} of daylight in October.
